web_title: 2. Business Model, Segment Mix & Real-World Deployments
book_title: Inside the Machine: Robots, Code, and Ad Screens
question: What does Kody Technolab actually sell across its robotics, software, and pDOOH lines, and where are its products deployed in the real world?

epigraph.quote: A robot in a trade-show booth is a marketing expense; a robot running twelve hours a day in a Dubai hypermarket is a business.
epigraph.author: Field Deployment Principle

web_blocks.html: Kody Technolab's audited accounts carry a major blind spot. The company reports under a single accounting segment: IT and IT-enabled services, software development, and tech solutions [7]. Management does not publish an audited revenue or profit split between IT services and robotics. Investors must therefore piece together the mix from product filings, subsidiary updates, and live field rollouts.

web_blocks.title: The Four Operating Pillars & Concrete Real-World Examples

web_blocks.html: In practice, Kody runs four product and service lines across India and the UAE. The firm states it has 200+ commercial robots deployed live and a pipeline of 1,500+ units [2]. Each line targets a distinct buyer and payment model.

web_blocks.takeaway: Commercial traction is shifting from one-off event demos (Athena, Dasher) toward retail ad fleets (Odigo in UAE malls) and contracted healthcare manufacturing (Medigo), though statutory accounts still bundle everything into one IT segment.

web_blocks.title: Walkthrough 1: How Odigo and Kody Media Monetize a Mall Floor

web_blocks.html: Consider a live rollout inside a LuLu Group International hypermarket in the UAE or an Indian mall [6]. Instead of bolting a static screen to a wall, Kody places Odigo on the floor. Odigo carries dual 32-inch touchscreens and uses LiDAR sensors to avoid shoppers [5]. Shoppers tap or speak to Odigo for aisle directions. At the same time, its moving screens play programmatic Digital Out-of-Home (pDOOH) ads. Kody Media Limited manages those ad slots in India, while Kody Middle East Holding LLC and Hypermedia run them in the UAE [2, 6]. Brands pay for impressions and footfall reach, turning the robot into a mobile ad node.

web_blocks.title: Walkthrough 2: Athena, Dasher, and Medigo in Institutional Settings

web_blocks.html: At public venues like the Tuneland Music Festival in GIFT City and the Gujarat Police Expo, Kody deployed Athena and Dasher [5]. Athena patrols perimeters with 360-degree UHD and thermal cameras to flag threats to a central desk [5]. Dasher handles automated tray and item delivery across venues [5]. In healthcare, Kody signed a three-year deal with Falcon Tech Robotics LLC (UAE) and Sccore AI Tech Diagnostic Limited (UAE) [7]. That pact makes Kody the exclusive global maker of Medigo, an AI rapid health-screening robot for clinics and wellness hubs [5, 7].

web_blocks.title: Geographic Mix and the Standalone-vs-Consolidated Gap

web_blocks.html: Historically, 80% to 90%+ of Kody's revenue came from India [7]. Exports to the UAE, US, UK, Canada, and Switzerland are now the main growth push [7]. In FY26, standalone sales reached ₹84.01 Cr with standalone net profit of ₹21.85 Cr [2]. Consolidated sales were ₹80 Cr, and consolidated net profit dropped to ₹17 Cr [1]. That ₹4.85 Cr profit gap proves that newer subsidiaries like Kody Media and overseas units are currently losing money as they build out fleets.

Kody also markets Skanda, an indigenous humanoid unveiled at the Vibrant Gujarat Summit [5]. Skanda serves mainly as an R&D showcase and public-engagement flagship. By contrast, Odigo and Medigo carry the real commercial weight across Gulf retail and healthcare [2, 6, 7]. Meanwhile, legacy software contracts still cushion parent-level cash flows while hardware fleets ramp up [2, 7].

web_blocks.title: Forensic Gap: Single-Segment Opacity
paragraphs: Kody Technolab lumps all revenue into one IT/software segment [7]. External analysts cannot verify from audited notes how much of H1 FY27's ₹62 Cr revenue came from IT services, how much came from hardware sales, and how much came from RaaS or pDOOH ads.

book_paragraphs: To see how Kody Technolab actually makes a rupee, you and I have to walk onto two very different floors: a software engineering bay in Ahmedabad and a hypermarket aisle in Dubai. On the statutory balance sheet, Kody still files under a single reporting segment called IT and IT-enabled services. That single-segment classification is the first thing you should underline in red ink, because it means the audited financials do not separate legacy software billing from robot hardware sales or advertising revenue. To understand the real mix, we have to trace the products on the ground.

Start with Odigo, arguably Kody's most commercially legible machine. Imagine walking into a LuLu Group hypermarket in the UAE or a busy Indian mall. Instead of passing a stationary poster, you encounter a waist-high autonomous unit gliding along a mapped path on LiDAR sensors, carrying two 32-inch touchscreens. You can tap the screen to find a store or ask a question, while brands buy programmatic ad slots on those moving displays through Kody Media in India or Hypermedia in the UAE. In theory, Odigo turns capital equipment into a recurring media asset.

Now walk over to Kody's second pillar: security and hospitality robots. At the Gujarat Police Expo and during the Tuneland Music Festival in GIFT City, Kody deployed Athena—an autonomous patrol unit fitted with 360-degree Ultra HD and thermal cameras—alongside Dasher, a multi-tray delivery robot. These deployments prove the hardware works in live, messy human crowds, not just laboratory videos. A third pillar, Skanda, is an indigenous AI humanoid showcased at the Vibrant Gujarat Summit, serving primarily as an interactive brand ambassador and R&D flagship.

A fourth pillar emerged through healthcare and international manufacturing: Medigo, an AI-powered rapid health-screening robot. Kody signed a three-year tripartite agreement with its UAE joint venture, Falcon Tech Robotics LLC, and Sccore AI Tech Diagnostic Limited to serve as Medigo's exclusive worldwide manufacturer. Alongside these hardware lines, Kody's original custom software, mobile app, and enterprise AI consulting business continues to serve domestic Indian corporates—which still account for roughly 80% to 90% of historical revenue—and clients in the US, UK, Canada, and Switzerland.

Here is the forensic clue hidden inside FY26's numbers. On a standalone basis, Kody reported ₹84.01 crore in revenue and ₹21.85 crore in net profit. Yet on a consolidated basis, sales were ₹80 crore and net profit dropped to ₹17 crore. That ₹4.85 crore profit gap tells you and I something vital: the parent company's core operations are profitable, while the newer subsidiaries—Kody Media, Kody Middle East, and the fleet buildout—are absorbing losses and inter-company eliminations as they scale. Until management breaks out segment-level revenue and unit economics, we are watching a hybrid engine whose true fuel mix remains partially obscured.

Let us walk through what that hybrid mix looks like in practice for a customer. Take the Medigo health-screening robot, which Kody manufactures under its three-year tripartite mandate in the UAE. A clinic or corporate wellness center installs Medigo to run rapid, multi-parameter preventive screenings. Kody earns revenue from manufacturing and exporting the hardware unit, plus ongoing software and AI diagnostic integration. Unlike a mall advertising robot, Medigo's economics depend on export fulfillment, regulatory reliability, and recurring diagnostic software licensing.

Contrast that with Athena and Dasher in domestic Indian environments. When Athena patrols a public festival like Tuneland in GIFT City or demonstrates perimeter surveillance at the Gujarat Police Expo, the buyer is typically a municipal body, law-enforcement agency, or large event operator. Those customers validate the technology and generate powerful media headlines, but government and institutional procurement cycles in India are notoriously slow to pay. That helps explain why Kody's debtor days climbed from 177 days to 192 days even as commercial activity accelerated.

Meanwhile, Kody's legacy software and enterprise AI division quietly acts as the financial stabilizer. Historically, 80% to 90% of Kody's revenue has been domestic, anchored by custom web, mobile, and AI-agent development. That software work carries high gross margins and minimal fixed-asset requirements. The central analytical puzzle of Chapter 2 is simple: how fast is the 200-plus-unit robotics fleet—and the stated 1,500-unit pipeline—scaling relative to legacy IT services, and at what consolidated operating margin will the two engines settle once the dust clears?

Until management publishes a formal segment note separating software services, hardware sales, and pDOOH media revenue, you and I have to treat consolidated margin compression as our primary thermometer. When H1 FY27 margins dropped to 19% while sales nearly doubled, that thermometer told us unmistakably that lower-margin hardware, EMS assembly, and early-stage media deployments are now driving a much larger share of the top line.

Think about why that distinction matters for your mental model of Kody. Software revenue scales with headcount and requires almost no fixed assets. Robotics manufacturing and pDOOH ad networks require factory tooling, component inventory, field technicians, and patient working capital. When both sit inside one unnamed segment, you must watch consolidated cash conversion and depreciation even more closely than headline sales growth.

At the same time, give credit where it is due: deploying over 200 commercial units across India and the UAE is no small feat for an SME founded in 2017. Most Indian robotics startups never leave the pilot stage. Kody's challenge now is proving that live deployments translate into high-margin, repeatable cash flow.

book_callouts.title: Follow the Consolidated-vs-Standalone Gap
book_callouts.text: When standalone PAT (₹21.85 Cr) exceeds consolidated PAT (₹17 Cr) by nearly ₹5 crore, the subsidiaries are burning cash to build the new business model. Always track consolidated cash conversion, not standalone headline margins.
